finding.claim: Authorization bypass on DELETE: `require_allowed` is an alias for the boolean predicate `is_allowed`, not `ensure_allowed`. Its return value is discarded, so the file is deleted for any caller, including unauthenticated ones.
finding.source: Any HTTP client sending DELETE /files/<fid> with any X-Session-User-Verified value, or none

trace.note: `from acl import is_allowed as require_allowed` imports the predicate under a name that implies it enforces
is_allowed returns a bool and never aborts
the bool result is ignored as a bare statement

finding.guards_checked: No other check on this route. rename_file correctly uses ensure_allowed, which calls abort(403), but delete_file does not. before_request only populates g.user and does not reject anyone.

verdict.guard_found: none effective: only before_request load_user (views.py:10-12) which just sets g.user; require_allowed is aliased to bool-returning is_allowed (views.py:4, acl.py:4-5) and its result is discarded at views.py:18
verdict.reason: views.py:4 aliases the bool predicate is_allowed (acl.py:5, no abort) as require_allowed, views.py:18 discards its result, so views.py:19 `del STORE[fid]` runs for any caller, including anonymous ones, as long as fid exists in STORE.

finding.claim: The identity used for every ACL decision is read from a client-supplied request header, `X-Session-User-Verified`. The app does no verification of its own, so unless a trusted proxy strips and overwrites the header, a client can impersonate any user, including a user who holds grants on a file.
finding.sink: ensure_allowed(g.user, f, "write") at views.py:26, which authorizes the rename write at views.py:27

trace.note: g.user is taken directly from the request header, with no session, signature or token validation
g.user is passed to ensure_allowed as the principal
grants are looked up by that user string

finding.guards_checked: No authentication middleware or signature check in the code. This is exploitable only if the app is reachable without a fronting proxy that sets and sanitises the header, which cannot be determined from this code.

verdict.guard_found: ensure_allowed (acl.py:8-10) correctly aborts 403 on the rename path (views.py:26), but it only checks grants for the header-supplied identity. No authentication or header sanitisation exists in the code, which has only views.py and acl.py.
verdict.reason: views.py:12 does take g.user straight from the X-Session-User-Verified header, and acl.py:5 keys grants on that string, so an anonymous client could impersonate a grantee if the app is exposed directly. The header name suggests a trusted proxy sets it, and nothing in this code shows whether one does.

finding.claim: STORE[fid] raises an unhandled KeyError when fid is unknown, so a request for a nonexistent id returns HTTP 500. Because the lookup runs before any permission check, the 500 versus 403 response reveals which file ids exist. This is a minor information leak and robustness issue.
finding.sink: STORE[fid] lookup in delete_file (views.py:17) and rename_file (views.py:25)

trace.note: direct dict indexing with no .get() or 404 handling

finding.guards_checked: No error handler or existence check. The impact is low.

verdict.guard_found: none for the KeyError: no .get(), no 404 handling, no errorhandler. The ACL calls at views.py:18 and 26 run after the lookup. Separately, views.py:4 aliases the bool-returning is_allowed (acl.py:4) as require_allowed, and views.py:18 discards its result.
verdict.reason: views.py:17 and views.py:25 index STORE[fid] directly before any ACL check, so an unknown fid raises an unhandled KeyError (HTTP 500). A known fid gets past the lookup, which lets an unauthenticated caller tell which ids exist. Rename returns 403 via ensure_allowed (acl.py:9-10). Delete behaves differently from the claim: views.py:18 discards the bool from is_allowed, so a known id is deleted with 200 rather than 403. That is a much more serious bug but is outside this finding.
